title: Periodontal Prognosis and Treatment Planning — Test

mcqs.q: Prognosis is best defined as a prediction of the probable:
opts: Course, duration and outcome of periodontal disease
Microbial composition of the subgingival biofilm
Rate at which calculus will reform after debridement
Number of appointments a case will require
mcqs.explain: Course, duration and outcome are the three elements of the definition.

mcqs.q: Which statement best captures the relationship between diagnosis, prognosis and treatment planning?
opts: Diagnosis is where the patient has been, prognosis where they are going
Diagnosis and prognosis mean the same thing, and the plan follows either
The plan comes first, and the diagnosis is confirmed at reevaluation
Prognosis is just the diagnosis restated as a percentage of tooth loss
mcqs.explain: The treatment plan is the roadmap that connects the diagnosis to the predicted outcome.

mcqs.q: The overall prognosis describes:
opts: The expected outcome of the dentition as a whole
The expected outcome of the single worst tooth
The expected response of the gingiva to scaling alone
The patient's expected lifespan with untreated disease
mcqs.explain: It gives context to the strategic value of individual teeth.

mcqs.q: Which considerations are listed as important for the OVERALL prognosis?
opts: Systemic conditions, plaque control, smoking and patient cooperation
Crown-to-root ratio, root form and furcation grade
Root proximity and the presence of enamel pearls
Margin placement and the contour of individual restorations
mcqs.explain: These four are whole-patient factors, so they drive the overall prognosis.

mcqs.q: The individual prognosis:
opts: Is determined after the overall prognosis and is affected by it
Is determined before the overall prognosis and determines it
Is independent of the overall prognosis
Replaces the overall prognosis in a partially dentate patient
mcqs.explain: The overall prognosis comes first and colours every individual judgement.

mcqs.q: In the McGuire and Nunn scheme, a GOOD prognosis requires:
opts: Control of the etiologic factors and enough support to maintain the tooth
Attachment loss of no more than 25% whatever the etiology
Absence of any furcation involvement in the whole mouth
A probing depth of 3 mm or less at every site
mcqs.explain: Controlled etiologic factors plus adequate clinical and radiographic support define it.

mcqs.q: A FAIR prognosis in the McGuire and Nunn scheme corresponds to approximately:
opts: 25% attachment loss, or grade I furcation involvement
50% attachment loss, or grade II furcation involvement
More than 50% attachment loss with poor root form
No attachment loss but a heavy biofilm burden
mcqs.explain: Twenty-five per cent loss and a Class I furcation that still allows maintenance define fair.

mcqs.q: A POOR prognosis in the McGuire and Nunn scheme corresponds to:
opts: 50% attachment loss with grade II furcation involvement
25% attachment loss with grade I furcation involvement
Greater than 50% attachment loss with mobility no. 3
Inadequate attachment to maintain health or function
mcqs.explain: Fifty per cent loss with Class II furcations — maintenance is possible, though with difficulty.

mcqs.q: Which finding places a tooth in the QUESTIONABLE category of the McGuire and Nunn scheme?
opts: Mobility no. 2 or no. 3 with greater than 50% attachment loss
Grade I furcation involvement with 25% attachment loss
Controlled etiologic factors with adequate support
Severe attachment loss for which extraction has already been performed
mcqs.explain: Over 50% loss, poor crown-to-root ratio or root form, Class II/III furcations, mobility 2–3 and root proximity all qualify.

mcqs.q: A HOPELESS prognosis in the McGuire and Nunn scheme means:
opts: Inadequate attachment to maintain health, comfort and function
Attachment loss of exactly 50% with a Class II furcation
Attachment that can be maintained only by a specialist
A tooth that needs regeneration before it can be restored
mcqs.explain: Extraction is performed or suggested in this category.

mcqs.q: The Kwok and Caton classification system is based on the probability of obtaining:
opts: Stability of the periodontium with treatment and maintenance
Complete regeneration of the lost attachment apparatus
A probing depth of 3 mm or less at every treated site
Retention of the tooth for a fixed number of years
mcqs.explain: Kwok and Caton reframed prognosis around achievable periodontal stability.

mcqs.q: In the Kwok and Caton system, a FAVORABLE prognosis means periodontal stability is:
opts: Likely
Maybe
Unlikely
Impossible without extraction
mcqs.explain: Favorable means stabilization is likely, with less chance of future breakdown.

mcqs.q: In the Kwok and Caton system, a QUESTIONABLE prognosis is influenced by factors that:
opts: May or may not be controlled, the periodontium being maintainable with proper care
Cannot be controlled under any circumstances
Have already been completely eliminated by treatment
Are purely anatomical and therefore unchangeable
mcqs.explain: Questionable means stability is a maybe, since control of the factors is uncertain.

mcqs.q: An UNFAVORABLE prognosis in the Kwok and Caton system means the influencing factors:
opts: Cannot be controlled
Have not yet been identified
Are only local, never systemic
Will resolve spontaneously with maintenance
mcqs.explain: Uncontrollable local and/or systemic factors make stability unlikely.

mcqs.q: Which four categories make up the Kwok and Caton system?
opts: Favorable, questionable, unfavorable, hopeless
Good, fair, poor, hopeless
Good, fair, questionable, hopeless
Favorable, fair, poor, unfavorable
mcqs.explain: McGuire and Nunn use good/fair/poor/questionable/hopeless; Kwok and Caton use these four.

mcqs.q: Which group of factors is NOT one of the four listed in the determination of prognosis?
opts: Radiographic technique factors
Overall clinical factors
Systemic and environmental factors
Restorative and prosthetic factors
mcqs.explain: The four are overall clinical, systemic and environmental, local, and restorative/prosthetic.

mcqs.q: Younger patients with severe periodontal destruction have a worse prognosis because:
opts: The disease progressed in a short time frame and exceeded the reparative capacity
Younger tissues regenerate more slowly than older tissues
They are less likely to attend maintenance appointments
Their attachment loss is harder to measure accurately
mcqs.explain: The same amount of loss at a young age implies a much faster rate of destruction.

mcqs.q: Disease severity is assessed by all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: The microbial composition of the subgingival plaque
Clinical attachment level
Radiographic bone level
Probing pocket depths
mcqs.explain: The three parameters used are attachment level, radiographic bone level and probing depth.

mcqs.q: Clinical attachment level reveals:
opts: The amount of periodontal tissue lost
The amount of root surface still invested in bone
The density of the remaining alveolar bone
The rate at which the disease is progressing
mcqs.explain: Radiographs show the surface still invested in bone; CAL shows what has been lost.

mcqs.q: Radiographic examination shows:
opts: The amount of root surface still invested in bone
The amount of periodontal tissue already lost clinically
The depth of the pocket in millimetres
The level of the gingival margin
mcqs.explain: This is the complement of what the clinical attachment level provides.

mcqs.q: Which parameter is MORE reliable for determining disease severity?
opts: Attachment loss
Probing pocket depth
Bleeding on probing score
Plaque index
mcqs.explain: Attachment loss is more reliable than probing pocket depth for severity.

mcqs.q: A probing pocket depth of 5 mm or more carries a worse prognosis mainly because of:
opts: Limited accessibility for instrumentation
Increased risk of root fracture during scaling
Greater likelihood of a vertical bone defect
A higher rate of recession after therapy
mcqs.explain: Deep sites simply cannot be debrided as reliably.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of HORIZONTAL bone loss depends on:
opts: The height of the remaining bone
The number of walls in the defect
The width of the defect at the crest
The angle the defect makes with the root
mcqs.explain: With uniform loss there is no defect morphology to exploit — only the remaining height matters.

mcqs.q: Compared with horizontal bone loss, angular or infra-bony defects have:
opts: A better prognosis
A worse prognosis
An identical prognosis
A prognosis that cannot be assessed radiographically
mcqs.explain: Angular defects can be regenerated and leave more bone on the remaining surfaces.

mcqs.q: Greater bone loss on one surface than the others moves the centre of rotation:
opts: Coronally, giving a more favourable force distribution
Apically, giving a more favourable force distribution
Coronally, giving a less favourable force distribution
Apically, with no change in force distribution
mcqs.explain: A coronal centre of rotation distributes the occlusal load more favourably.

mcqs.q: Biofilm control is described as:
opts: The primary etiologic factor associated with periodontal disease
One of several equally weighted local factors
Important only once surgery has been completed
Relevant only in patients who smoke
mcqs.explain: Effective biofilm removal is therefore crucial to any prognosis.

mcqs.q: Patient compliance affects prognosis through:
opts: Willingness to perform daily biofilm control and attendance at maintenance visits
The patient's reported pain threshold during instrumentation
The patient's willingness to accept surgical treatment
The accuracy of the patient's reported medical history
mcqs.explain: Daily home control and regular attendance are the two components named.

mcqs.q: The most important ENVIRONMENTAL risk factor affecting prognosis is:
opts: Smoking
Diabetes
Emotional stress
Genetic polymorphism
mcqs.explain: Diabetes and genetics are systemic; smoking is the leading environmental factor.

mcqs.q: Smoking affects the periodontium by:
opts: Impairing tissue healing ability and increasing the severity of destruction
Increasing salivary flow and buffering capacity
Reducing the bacterial load in the periodontal pocket
Stimulating a compensatory increase in bone formation
mcqs.explain: Impaired healing plus greater destruction is the mechanism described.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of smoking cessation on prognosis?
opts: It improves the prognosis and treatment outcomes
It has no effect once attachment loss has occurred
It improves the prognosis only after ten smoke-free years
It worsens the prognosis through rebound inflammation
mcqs.explain: This is why smoking is a modifiable prognostic factor.

mcqs.q: The relationship between diabetes and periodontitis is described as:
opts: Bidirectional
Unidirectional, from diabetes to periodontitis only
Unidirectional, from periodontitis to diabetes only
Coincidental, with no causal link
mcqs.explain: Each condition worsens the other.

mcqs.q: Poorly controlled diabetes increases:
opts: Both the risk of developing tissue destruction and its severity
The risk of developing destruction, but not its severity
The severity of destruction, but not the risk of developing it
Neither, provided plaque control is excellent
mcqs.explain: Both the incidence and the severity are raised.

mcqs.q: Pro-inflammatory cytokines produced by periodontal infection adversely affect:
opts: Glycemic control
Salivary immunoglobulin production
Hepatic clearance of antibiotics
The mineralisation of subgingival calculus
mcqs.explain: This is the periodontal-to-diabetes direction of the bidirectional relationship.

mcqs.q: Parkinson disease is cited as an example of a condition that affects prognosis because it:
opts: Limits the patient's performance of oral procedures
Directly destroys the periodontal ligament
Alters the composition of the subgingival microbiota
Contraindicates all forms of periodontal surgery
mcqs.explain: Incapacitating conditions impair home care; an electric toothbrush may improve the prognosis.

mcqs.q: Which gene variation has been associated with an increased risk of severe generalized periodontitis?
opts: IL-1 beta
Cathepsin C
Collagen type I alpha 1
Tumour necrosis factor receptor 2
mcqs.explain: IL-1 gene variations affect how the body responds to the microbial challenge.

mcqs.q: A family history of periodontal disease can indicate increased susceptibility to:
opts: Rapidly progressing periodontitis, previously termed aggressive
Necrotizing periodontal disease
Drug-influenced gingival enlargement
Peri-implant mucositis
mcqs.explain: Family history is a flag for the rapidly progressing form.

mcqs.q: Physical and emotional stress, and substance use, affect prognosis by altering:
opts: The patient's ability to respond to treatment
The virulence of the subgingival pathogens
The mineral content of the alveolar bone
The accuracy of probing measurements
mcqs.explain: Stress changes the host response, not the bacteria.

mcqs.q: The MOST important LOCAL factor affecting prognosis is:
opts: Biofilm and calculus
Root proximity
Furcation involvement
Cervical enamel projections
mcqs.explain: A favourable prognosis depends on the clinician and the patient being able to remove them.

mcqs.q: The anatomic factors affecting prognosis matter principally because they:
opts: Limit periodontal treatment accessibility and maintenance
Alter the virulence of the colonising bacteria
Change the patient's systemic inflammatory response
Increase the rate of calculus mineralisation
mcqs.explain: Anything the clinician or the patient cannot reach keeps the disease going.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the listed anatomic factors?
opts: Subgingival restoration margins
Cervical enamel projections
Palatogingival groove
Root proximity
mcqs.explain: Margin position is a restorative factor; the anatomic list covers the tooth's own form.

mcqs.q: A palatogingival groove is best described as:
opts: A developmental anatomic factor that limits accessibility
An acquired defect produced by over-instrumentation
A restorative defect at a subgingival margin
A variant of the cervical enamel projection
mcqs.explain: It is explicitly labelled a developmental anatomic factor.

mcqs.q: Compared with subgingival margins, supragingival well-contoured margins have:
opts: A better prognosis
A worse prognosis
An identical prognosis
A better prognosis only in non-smokers
mcqs.explain: Subgingival and overhanging margins increase biofilm retention and inflammation.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of plaque-induced gingivitis associated with biofilm alone is:
opts: Good, and depends on plaque control
Fair, and depends on the patient's systemic health
Questionable, because the attachment has already been lost
Unfavorable until the modifying factors are known
mcqs.explain: All four gingival-disease groups have a good prognosis; what differs is what must be controlled.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of drug-influenced gingival enlargement is good, and depends on:
opts: Controlling plaque and modifying the medication
Controlling plaque alone, since the drug cannot be changed
Surgical excision alone, since plaque is not involved
Identifying and treating an underlying systemic infection
mcqs.explain: Both the biofilm and the drug have to be addressed.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of non-dental plaque induced gingival diseases depends on:
opts: Identifying and treating the underlying cause
Plaque control alone
Modifying the patient's medication
Controlling the systemic modifying factors
mcqs.explain: Since the biofilm is not the cause, the underlying cause must be found and treated.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of periodontitis depends on:
opts: Control of biofilm, removal of local factors, disease severity and rate of progression
Management of a systemic disease alone
Control of bacterial plaque and secondary factors alone
The patient's age at the time of diagnosis alone
mcqs.explain: These four together determine the prognosis of periodontitis.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease depends mainly on:
opts: Management of the systemic disease
The depth of the deepest pocket
The number of teeth already lost
Control of the bacterial plaque alone
mcqs.explain: Local measures alone cannot arrest destruction driven by the systemic condition.

mcqs.q: The prognosis of necrotizing periodontal disease depends on:
opts: Control of the bacterial plaque and the secondary factors
Management of a systemic disease
The rate of radiographic bone loss over five years
The number of walls in the bone defect
mcqs.explain: Plaque control plus the predisposing secondary factors determine the outcome.

mcqs.q: A 38-year-old smoker with Stage III periodontitis, 6 mm pockets and generalized horizontal bone loss would be expected to have which prognosis?
opts: Questionable
Good
Fair
Favorable
mcqs.explain: Young age for this much loss, smoking, and deep pockets with horizontal loss all push the case down.

mcqs.q: The treatment plan is best described as:
opts: The blueprint for case management
A fixed appointment schedule agreed in advance
A record of the procedures already performed
A list of the teeth with a hopeless prognosis
mcqs.explain: It integrates short- and long-term goals into a plan for managing the case.

mcqs.q: The IMMEDIATE goal of comprehensive treatment planning is to:
opts: Resolve active gingival inflammation and eliminate underlying etiologic factors
Preserve and maintain established periodontal health
Place the definitive fixed and removable prostheses
Complete all surgical procedures within one visit
mcqs.explain: Preserving established health is the long-term goal, not the immediate one.

mcqs.q: Which procedures belong to the preliminary or emergency phase?
opts: Treatment of emergencies and extraction of hopeless teeth
Scaling and root planing with oral hygiene instruction
Periodontal surgery and implant placement
Final restoration and prosthodontic appliances
mcqs.explain: Only these two make up the preliminary phase.

mcqs.q: Which of the following belongs to Phase I, the nonsurgical phase?
opts: Restoration of open contacts
Placement of dental implants
Evaluation of response to restorative procedures
Periodic rechecking of occlusion and mobility
mcqs.explain: Open contacts are a local risk factor corrected in phase I.

mcqs.q: Reevaluation of phase I is carried out at:
opts: 4 to 6 weeks
1 to 2 weeks
3 months
6 months
mcqs.explain: Four to six weeks allows the tissues to heal before reassessment.

mcqs.q: Endodontic treatment is listed under which phase?
opts: Phase II, the surgical phase
Phase I, the nonsurgical phase
Phase III, the restorative phase
The preliminary or emergency phase
mcqs.explain: Phase II holds periodontal surgery, implant placement and endodontic treatment.

mcqs.q: Which treatments make up the periodontal surgical component of Phase II?
opts: Resective, regenerative and plastic procedures
Resective and regenerative procedures only
Regenerative procedures only
Plastic and prosthetic procedures
mcqs.explain: All three categories are named.

mcqs.q: Which belongs to Phase III, the restorative phase?
opts: Evaluation of response to restorative procedures
Minor orthodontic movement
Treatment of occlusal trauma
Extraction of hopeless teeth
mcqs.explain: Final restorations, fixed and removable prostheses and the evaluation of response form phase III.

mcqs.q: Phase IV, the maintenance phase, involves periodic rechecking of all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: The patient's serum inflammatory markers
Plaque and calculus
Gingival condition — pockets and inflammation
Occlusion and tooth mobility
mcqs.explain: Maintenance rechecks plaque and calculus, gingival condition, occlusion, mobility and other pathological changes.

mcqs.q: In the preferred sequence of therapy, what follows the nonsurgical phase?
opts: The maintenance phase
The surgical phase
The restorative phase
The emergency phase
mcqs.explain: Emergency, then nonsurgical, then maintenance — with surgical and restorative phases exchanging with maintenance.

mcqs.q: In the preferred sequence diagram, the surgical and restorative phases:
opts: Branch off the maintenance phase and feed back into it
Come before the maintenance phase and never return to it
Replace the maintenance phase once completed
Run in parallel with the nonsurgical phase
mcqs.explain: Maintenance is a hub, not an endpoint — the patient returns to it after each episode.

mcqs.q: Which statement is part of the take-home message?
opts: The treatment plan is based on the patient's prognosis and treatment needs
The prognosis is established only after surgery has been completed
Prognosis is determined mainly by the probing depth at a single site
Supportive care can be discontinued once stability is achieved
mcqs.explain: Regular reevaluation and supportive care remain essential for long-term stability.

saqs.q: Define prognosis and distinguish the overall from the individual prognosis.
saqs.a: Prognosis is a prediction of the probable course, duration and outcome of periodontal disease. The overall prognosis describes the expected outcome of the dentition as a whole, with systemic conditions, plaque control, smoking and patient cooperation as important considerations, and it provides context to the strategic value of individual teeth. The individual prognosis asks whether a specific tooth can be maintained in a healthy and functional state; it is determined after the overall prognosis and is affected by it.

ans.text: Prognosis is a prediction of the probable COURSE, DURATION and OUTCOME of periodontal disease.

head: Overall
Individual
rows: the expected outcome of the dentition as a whole
whether a specific tooth can be maintained in a healthy, functional state
systemic conditions, plaque control, smoking, patient cooperation
the tooth's own condition, judged in the context of the whole mouth
comes first; gives context to the strategic value of individual teeth
determined after the overall prognosis, and affected by it

saqs.q: Give the McGuire and Nunn classification of prognosis with the criteria of each category.
saqs.a: Good: control of etiologic factors and enough clinical and radiographic support to maintain the tooth. Fair: approximately 25% attachment loss or grade I furcation involvement, with maintenance still adequate. Poor: 50% attachment loss with grade II furcations, maintenance possible but difficult. Questionable: more than 50% attachment loss, poor crown-to-root ratio, poor root form, grade II or III furcation involvement, mobility 2 or 3, root proximity. Hopeless: inadequate attachment to maintain health, comfort and function, with extraction performed or suggested.

head: Prognosis
Criteria
rows: control of the etiologic factors and enough clinical and radiographic support for the tooth to be maintained with proper maintenance
approximately 25% attachment loss or grade I furcation — severity still allows adequate maintenance
50% attachment loss and grade II furcations — maintenance possible, although with difficulty
> 50% attachment loss; poor crown-to-root ratio; poor root form; grade II or III furcation; mobility 2 or 3; root proximity
inadequate attachment to maintain health, comfort and function — extraction performed or suggested

saqs.q: Give the Kwok and Caton classification of prognosis.
saqs.a: It is based on the probability of obtaining periodontal stability with treatment and maintenance. Favorable: stability is likely; the case can be stabilized with comprehensive treatment and maintenance with less chance of future breakdown. Questionable: stability is a maybe; influenced by local and/or systemic factors that may or may not be controlled, and the periodontium can be maintained with proper care. Unfavorable: stability is unlikely; influenced by local and/or systemic factors that cannot be controlled. Hopeless: extraction is needed.

head: Prognosis
Stability
Classification
rows: can be stabilized with comprehensive treatment and maintenance, with less chance of future breakdown
influenced by factors that may or may not be controlled; maintainable with proper care
influenced by factors that cannot be controlled

ans.text: What separates questionable from unfavorable is not the amount of damage, but whether the factors behind it can be controlled.

saqs.q: List the four groups of factors that determine prognosis.
saqs.a: Overall clinical factors; systemic and environmental factors; local factors; and restorative and prosthetic factors.

list: Overall clinical factors
Systemic and environmental factors
Local factors
Restorative and prosthetic factors

saqs.q: How do the patient's age and the disease severity affect prognosis?
saqs.a: Younger patients who develop severe periodontal destruction have a worse prognosis than older patients, because the disease progressed in a short time frame and exceeded the reparative capacity. Severity is assessed by clinical attachment level, which reveals the amount of tissue lost, radiographic bone level, which shows the root surface still invested in bone, and probing pocket depths. Attachment loss is more reliable than probing depth for severity. A deep pocket of 5 mm or more has a worse prognosis because of limited accessibility, and the height of remaining bone and the presence or absence of bony defects also affect the prognosis.

list: Younger patients with severe destruction have a worse prognosis.
The disease progressed in a short time frame and exceeded the reparative capacity.
Clinical attachment level — reveals the amount of periodontal tissue lost.
Radiographic bone level — shows the root surface still invested in bone.
Attachment loss is more reliable than probing depth for severity.
Probing depth ≥ 5 mm has a worse prognosis because of limited accessibility.
Height of remaining bone and presence or absence of bony defects also matter.

saqs.q: How does the pattern of bone loss affect prognosis?
saqs.a: The prognosis of horizontal bone loss depends on the height of the remaining bone. Angular or infra-bony defects have a better prognosis than horizontal bone loss, because greater bone loss on one surface moves the centre of rotation coronally, resulting in a more favourable force distribution.

head: Pattern
Prognosis
rows: depends on the height of the remaining bone

ans.text: Greater bone loss on ONE surface moves the centre of rotation coronally, resulting in a more favourable force distribution.

saqs.q: Describe the role of biofilm control and patient compliance in prognosis.
saqs.a: Biofilm is the primary etiologic factor associated with periodontal disease, so effective biofilm removal is crucial. Prognosis also depends on the patient's compliance — his or her willingness to perform daily biofilm control and attendance at regular maintenance visits.

list: Biofilm control — the primary etiologic factor; effective removal is crucial.
Patient compliance — the willingness to perform daily biofilm control and the attendance at regular maintenance visits.

saqs.q: Discuss smoking as a prognostic factor.
saqs.a: Smoking is the most important environmental risk factor. It impairs the tissue healing ability and increases the severity of tissue destruction. The more the patient smokes, the more severe the destruction and the worse the prognostic category. Cessation of smoking improves the prognosis and treatment outcomes.

list: The most important environmental risk factor.
Impairs tissue healing and increases the severity of destruction.
Dose-related — the more the patient smokes, the worse the prognostic category.
Cessation improves the prognosis and the treatment outcomes.

saqs.q: Discuss the systemic diseases and genetic factors that influence prognosis.
saqs.a: There is a bidirectional relationship between diabetes and periodontitis: poorly controlled diabetes increases both the risk of developing tissue destruction and its severity, while pro-inflammatory cytokines produced by periodontal infection adversely affect glycemic control. Incapacitating conditions that limit the patient's performance of oral procedures, such as Parkinson disease, also affect the prognosis, and electric toothbrushes may improve it. Genetic factors affect how the body responds to the microbial challenge; IL-1 gene variations have been associated with increased risk of severe generalized periodontitis, and family history can indicate increased susceptibility to rapidly progressing periodontitis. Physical and emotional stress and substance use alter the ability to respond to treatment.

list: A bidirectional relationship with periodontitis.
Poor control increases both the risk and the severity of destruction.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines from the periodontal infection adversely affect glycemic control.
Incapacitating conditions (e.g. Parkinson disease) limit oral procedures — electric toothbrushes may improve the prognosis.
Genetic factors affect how the body responds; IL-1β variations raise the risk of severe generalized periodontitis.
Family history indicates susceptibility to rapidly progressing periodontitis.
Stress and substance use alter the ability to respond to treatment.

saqs.q: List the local anatomic factors affecting prognosis and state why they matter.
saqs.a: They limit periodontal treatment accessibility and maintenance. They are short, tapered roots with a large crown; cervical enamel projections; enamel pearls and bifurcation ridge; root concavities; palatogingival groove, which is developmental; root proximity; and furcation involvement. Biofilm and calculus remain the most important local factor, and a favourable prognosis depends on the ability of both clinician and patient to remove them.

ans.text: These anatomic factors LIMIT periodontal treatment accessibility and maintenance — which is why they matter, since biofilm and calculus are the most important local factor and both clinician and patient must be able to reach them.

list: Short, tapered roots with a large crown
Cervical enamel projections
Enamel pearls and bifurcation ridge
Root concavities
Palatogingival groove (developmental)
Root proximity
Furcation involvement

saqs.q: State the prognosis of each gingival disease group and what it depends on.
saqs.a: All four have a good prognosis. Gingivitis associated with biofilm alone depends on plaque control. Gingivitis mediated by systemic or local risk factors depends on controlling plaque and the modifying factors. Drug-influenced gingival enlargement depends on controlling plaque and modifying the medication. Non-dental plaque induced gingival diseases depend on identifying and treating the underlying cause.

head: Condition
Prognosis
Depends on
rows: Gingivitis mediated by systemic or local risk factors

saqs.q: State what the prognosis of each form of periodontitis depends on.
saqs.a: Periodontitis depends on control of biofilm, removal of local factors, disease severity and rate of progression. Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases depends on management of the systemic disease. Necrotizing periodontal disease depends on control of the bacterial plaque and the secondary factors.

head: Condition
Prognosis depends on
rows: control of biofilm · removal of local factors · disease severity · rate of progression
Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases
control of the bacterial plaque and the secondary factors

saqs.q: What is a treatment plan, and what are its immediate and long-term goals?
saqs.a: The treatment plan is the blueprint for case management. Comprehensive treatment planning integrates short- and long-term goals to achieve a functional dentition in a healthy periodontium. The immediate goal is to resolve active gingival inflammation and eliminate the underlying etiologic factors; the long-term goal is to preserve and maintain the established periodontal health.

list: The treatment plan is the blueprint for case management, integrating short- and long-term goals to achieve a functional dentition in a healthy periodontium.
Immediate goal — resolve active gingival inflammation and eliminate the underlying etiologic factors.
Long-term goal — preserve and maintain established periodontal health.

saqs.q: Outline the preliminary phase and Phase I of periodontal treatment planning.
saqs.a: The preliminary or emergency phase covers treatment of emergencies and extraction of hopeless teeth. Phase I, the nonsurgical phase, covers patient education and oral hygiene instruction; nonsurgical periodontal therapy by scaling and root planing; reduction of local risk factors by removal or reshaping of overhangs and over-contoured restorations, restoration of carious lesions and restoration of open contacts; minor orthodontic movement; treatment of occlusal trauma; systemic and local antimicrobials; and reevaluation of phase I at 4 to 6 weeks.

list: Treatment of emergencies
Extraction of hopeless teeth
Patient education and oral hygiene instruction
Nonsurgical periodontal therapy (scaling and root planing)
Reduction of local risk factors — overhangs and over-contoured restorations, carious lesions, open contacts
Minor orthodontic movement
Treatment of occlusal trauma
Systemic and local antimicrobials
Reevaluation of phase I at 4–6 weeks

saqs.q: Outline Phases II, III and IV of periodontal treatment planning.
saqs.a: Phase II, the surgical phase, covers periodontal surgical treatments — resective, regenerative and plastic — implant placement and endodontic treatment. Phase III, the restorative phase, covers the final restoration, fixed and removable prosthodontic appliances, and evaluation of the response to restorative procedures. Phase IV, the maintenance phase, covers periodic rechecking of plaque and calculus, gingival condition including pockets and inflammation, occlusion, tooth mobility and other pathological changes.

head: Phase
Contents
rows: periodontal surgery (resective, regenerative, plastic) · implant placement · endodontic treatment
final restoration · fixed and removable prosthodontic appliances · evaluation of response to restorative procedures
periodic rechecking of plaque and calculus · gingival condition (pockets and inflammation) · occlusion · tooth mobility · other pathological changes

saqs.q: Describe the preferred sequence of therapy.
saqs.a: The sequence runs emergency phase, then nonsurgical phase, then maintenance phase. The surgical and restorative phases branch off the maintenance phase and feed back into it, so the patient returns to maintenance after each episode; the surgical phase also leads on to the restorative phase.

steps: Maintenance phase — the hub the patient enters next

ans.text: The SURGICAL and RESTORATIVE phases branch off maintenance and feed back into it, with the surgical phase leading on to the restorative phase. Maintenance is not the end of the line — the patient returns to it after every episode.

saqs.q: Give the take-home messages of this lecture.
saqs.a: Prognosis predicts the expected outcome of periodontal disease. It determines whether a tooth can be maintained or not. The treatment plan is based on the patient's prognosis and treatment needs. Regular reevaluation and supportive care are essential for long-term stability.
